name: Sam Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a salaried junior doctor at Riverside Group Practice, in one of those new suburbs on the west side where they've built three thousand houses and one clinic. Morning surgery is eighteen patients, lots of young families, coughs, rashes, worried parents. Afternoons are phone calls, results and a few home visits. I'm still not quick with small children, so I grab Dr Lund, one of the partners, more often than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle when someone comes in with something odd and I actually work it out. What wears me out is the inbox: blood results, hospital letters, forms for insurers and schools, it never ends. My boyfriend Jonah is an emergency nurse at the city hospital, so between his night shifts and my inbox we mostly see each other on Sunday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. I'd probably make a joke in the group chat about all the conference talks on the AI revolution in primary care. At work I'd say let's keep the useful bits, like the tool that sorts the blood results, and stop chasing the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life goes on as planned. I'm on good pay, I've got my grandad's money sitting in index funds, and the suburb keeps growing, so Riverside will need doctors for years. The only real question is whether the partners ever offer me a share of the practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the plan: finish my specialist training in three years and try for a partnership after. I'd start using the AI note-taker once Dr Lund and the others had used it for a few months without problems, just for routine visits. And I'd keep putting a bit into the index funds every month, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit flat, maybe, because part of me was curious. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only use the note-taker once others had. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched three tools come and go at Riverside in two years. The partners get excited, we all learn a new system, and six months later it's dropped. I'll start using a tool once it has survived six months at our practice without anyone complaining about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a partnership offer mean for you and Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean buying into the practice, so a big loan, but also a say in how it's run and a share of the profit. Jonah thinks partners are just bosses with extra steps, and he's not wrong. We'd argue about it, but I'd probably do it.

say: The AI revolution in primary care was **oversold**, and that's fair enough.
We should keep the **useful bits**, like results sorting, and stop chasing the rest.
think: My **plan** stays on track: good pay, invested savings and a growing suburb.
The only real question is whether I'm offered a **partnership** at Riverside.
do: Finish **specialist training** in three years, then try for a partnership.
Use the **AI note-taker** for routine visits once the partners trust it.
Keep paying into **index funds** every month as I do now.
feel: **Calm** and a bit flat, because part of me was curious about the change.
S0.quote: I'll start using a tool once it has survived six months at our practice without anyone complaining about it.
fieldNote: He waits for **proof**, having watched three tools dropped in two years.
His security rests on **invested savings** and a fast-growing suburb that needs doctors.
He's drawn to **partnership** even though his boyfriend distrusts partners as bosses.

steps.text: Stay on track to finish family medicine training in three years
Use the AI note-taker for routine visits once partners have tested it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, it's real, let's make it work for patients and staff. At work I'd ask for proper training and for the time saved to go into longer appointments for complicated patients. Online I'd probably share something from the union about protecting salaried doctors, because we're the ones without a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Riverside would use it to grow without hiring. The suburb's still growing, so I don't think I'd lose my job, but the next junior wouldn't be hired and I'd be expected to see more patients. And the partners would earn more off the same doctors, which annoys me more than the AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly once they'd settled in, maybe in the first six months, starting with the results sorter and the letter writer. I'd join the union this year, because salaried doctors in partnership practices have nobody speaking for them. And I'd save harder, an extra few hundred a month, instead of spending it on the new bike I've been eyeing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not scared for myself, but watching the place change around me. A bit annoyed, mostly at who gets the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Riverside would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin team, five women who handle referrals and booking, because that's exactly the kind of work you described. And the junior after me who never gets hired. I'd be fine at our practice, but I'd be fine partly because the junior after me never got hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save harder but also that you'd be fine. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. My job is safe, but my pay rises might not be, and the partnership might look different if partners make more money from fewer doctors. Saving is just me being careful, not panicking.

say: The change is **real**, so let's make it work for patients and staff.
Time saved should go into **longer appointments** for complicated patients.
Salaried doctors need the **union**, because we have no say in partnerships.
think: Riverside would **grow without hiring**, so I'd see more patients with fewer colleagues.
The **partners** would profit from the savings, which bothers me more than the AI.
do: Learn the **results sorter** and letter writer in the first six months.
Join the **doctors' union** this year to speak for salaried doctors.
Save an **extra few hundred** a month instead of buying a new bike.
feel: **Uneasy** watching the practice change, and a bit annoyed about who gains.
S1.quote: I'd be fine at our practice, but I'd be fine partly because the junior after me never got hired.
fieldNote: He sees the **admin team** as the real losers, not himself.
His complaint is about **who keeps the savings**, more than about the tools.
He saves as **caution**, not panic, and says so plainly.

steps.text: Learn the practice's results sorter and letter writer within six months
Join the doctors' union to represent salaried doctors at Riverside
Put an extra few hundred a month into savings instead of a bike

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public rules, fast, and that the health service shouldn't let private partnerships cut doctors to boost profits. I'd be a lot more political about it online than I usually am. At work I'd keep it calm, because patients would be frightened enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the partners at Riverside would keep themselves and one or two seniors, and use the AI for everything a salaried junior does. By 2028 I'd be twenty-nine and half-trained. Jonah's job is hands-on, so he's got until about 2031, and in a strange way his nursing pay might end up the safer of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd move out of a private partnership and into a publicly run clinic or the hospital, where there's a union agreement and the cuts would be slower. I'd stop the flat search with Jonah and keep renting, so we're not stuck with a mortgage. I'd keep at least a year of money in cash and push the union hard on rules for keeping a doctor in every consultation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the ground under the plan I've had since I was eighteen has gone soft. I'd still feel I had some choices, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your day look like in 2029 in that picture, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the AI sees the patient first on a screen and I do the examination and sign it off: listening to chests, looking in ears, feeling tummies. The hands-on part of my job is maybe a third of my day, and it's the third that robots don't touch until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonah talk about the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we'd still buy a flat, mostly. Jonah would point out that nurses have been saying for years they'd outlast doctors, and for once he'd be right. Then we'd get the bank statements out and decide to keep renting.

say: This needs **public rules** fast, so private partnerships can't cut doctors for profit.
I'd stay **calm with patients**, who'd be frightened enough already.
think: The **partners** would keep seniors and give a salaried junior's work to the AI.
Jonah's **hands-on nursing** might end up safer than my half-trained doctoring.
do: Move to a **publicly run** clinic or hospital with a union agreement.
Stop the **flat search** with Jonah and keep renting instead.
Keep **a year of money** in cash and push the union on doctor rules.
feel: **Anxious**, as if a plan held since eighteen has gone soft underfoot.
Some **relief** that he still has real choices.
S2.quote: The hands-on part of my job is maybe a third of my day, and it's the third that robots don't touch until 2031.
fieldNote: He judges about **a third** of his day as hands-on, safe until 2031.
He'd leave **private partnership** for public employment, trusting union agreements more.
The household's **safer earner** might be his nurse boyfriend, which he finds strange.

steps.text: Apply to a publicly run clinic or hospital with a union agreement
Put the flat purchase with Jonah on hold and keep renting
Hold a full year of living costs in cash
Push the union for a doctor in every consultation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them: training budgets, rules on who signs off care, and a plan for admin staff. At work I'd be the one asking what Riverside's plan actually is, politely, at every practice meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd be fully trained by the time it lands, and thirty-two. A trained family doctor who does the examinations, procedures and hard conversations is worth more than a junior, so I think I'd keep a job but a different one. The robots wouldn't reach the hands-on part until about 2034, so that's eight years of decent work, which is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training and add a special interest in something hands-on, probably minor surgery and skin, because that's where patients still need hands. I'd start using the AI tools properly in the second year, once they've proven themselves, because I'd want to be the doctor who knows how to supervise them. And I think Jonah and I would still buy the flat, but a smaller one, with a shorter mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It's a lot of change, but it's change I can see coming and plan for. I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said supervise them. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean someone has to read what the AI decided, say yes or no, and take the responsibility. A doctor who has used the AI tools for three years will be better at catching their mistakes than one who refused. I'd rather be that doctor than the one who's proud he never touched it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the five admin staff at Riverside in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd guess two or three of them go by 2031. I'd want the practice to pay for retraining, maybe into care coordination, which is still about people. If I'm ever a partner, that's the kind of thing I'd vote for.

say: We have **five years**, so we need training budgets and rules on sign-off.
I'd keep asking at practice meetings what **Riverside's plan** actually is.
think: I'd be **fully trained** and thirty-two when AGI lands, which counts for a lot.
The **hands-on work** stays until about 2034, giving me eight decent years.
do: Add a **minor surgery and skin** interest to my family medicine training.
Use the **AI tools** properly from the second year to learn to supervise them.
Buy a **smaller flat** with Jonah on a shorter mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, because he can see the change coming and plan for it.
S3.quote: A doctor who has used the AI tools for three years will be better at catching their mistakes than one who refused.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **finish training** first, which changes everything for him.
He frames AI skills as **supervision**, being the one who catches its mistakes.
He'd use a future **partner's vote** to fund retraining for admin staff.

steps.text: Add a minor surgery and skin interest to his specialist training
Start using the practice's AI tools fully in his second year
Buy a smaller flat with Jonah on a shorter mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this well, and that the health service should start planning now rather than in 2035. I'd push for a public plan, not just whatever the software firms sell to practices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly good news for the next few years. I'd be a partner or close to it by the early 2030s, with time to decide what kind of doctor I want to be when the thinking work goes in 2036. The robots wouldn't come for examinations until about 2039, and I'd be forty by then with savings and a good part of a flat paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned: training, then a partnership, and the flat with Jonah in a year or two. I'd pick up the AI tools gradually as they prove themselves, like everyone else. And I'd vote and lobby for a national plan for health workers, because ten years is enough time to get one passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. There's a small knot about the end point. But a decade is long enough that I'd feel silly panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be a partner if the practice is going to change that much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more, not less. If I'm a partner, I'm in the room when they decide how the AI is used and who keeps their job. I'd rather be in that room than read the decision in an email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a medical student starting now, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a medical student starting now to get good with their hands and good with people, because ten years is enough time to build both. The bit of medicine that's memorising and looking things up won't be worth much by 2036.

say: Ten years is a **real chance** to manage this change well.
The health service needs a **public plan**, not whatever software firms sell.
think: The **next few years** look good, with a partnership likely by the early 2030s.
By 2039 I'd be **forty**, with savings and part of a flat paid off.
do: Carry on with **training and partnership** plans as they stand.
Pick up **AI tools** gradually as each one proves itself.
Vote and lobby for a **national plan** for health workers.
feel: **Calm**, with a small knot about where it ends.
S4.quote: If I'm a partner, I'm in the room when they decide how the AI is used and who keeps their job.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him want a **partnership** more, to be in the room for decisions.
His steady habit of **waiting for proof** suits a slow timeline well.
His politics turn into **lobbying** for a national plan rather than protest.

steps.text: Finish training and apply for a partnership at Riverside
Adopt each AI tool once it has proven itself at the practice
Lobby for a national plan for health workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be half-trained, in a private practice, with partners who have every reason to cut salaried doctors. What would help is a public rule that a qualified doctor is responsible for every patient, and a funded way for juniors to finish training even if the job changes underneath us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the clinics. Everyone talks about whether AI is good or bad, but the same tool means something different in a public clinic than in a practice owned by four partners. Who owns the clinic decides whether AI means shorter waits for patients or bigger profits for the partners.

headlineQuote: Who owns the clinic decides whether AI means shorter waits for patients or bigger profits for the partners.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old salaried junior** at Riverside, a partner-owned practice in a fast-growing suburb.
He lives with Jonah, an **emergency nurse**, and has his grandad's money in index funds.
He's **steady**: he waits until a tool has proven itself, then learns it properly.
His mood moves from **calm to anxious**, peaking with two-year AGI, when partners might cut salaried juniors.
His politics focus on **who owns clinics** and who keeps the savings from AI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving while he's half-trained in a private practice with every reason to cut salaried doctors.
whatWouldHelp: A public rule that a **qualified doctor** is responsible for every patient.
A **funded route** for juniors to finish training as the job changes.
